extracted.intended_audience: educated general readers and literary readers/critics
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for recognizing genuine vs. sham admiration of literary works and for forming independent, honest critical judgment rather than socially driven or learned pretense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid pretense / sham admiration
rubrics_metrics.description: Pretense is prominent in civilized communities and, after a while, 'becomes systematized, gathers strength from numbers and impunity, and rears its head in such a manner as to suggest it has some body and substance.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-patterns: praising works from habit, fashion, or social imitation rather than genuine feeling. Examples in the text: universal praise of certain 'standard' books without real knowledge; people lauding classics they have never read. Scoring note: admiration grounded in knowledge and feeling scores higher than socially inherited or automatic praise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not mistake acquisition of a language for appreciation
rubrics_metrics.description: Many expend all their intelligence upon the mere acquisition of a foreign language and, as a result, 'the acquisition of ideas is very difficult, and when conveyed in a foreign language is impossible.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-pattern: quoting foreign phrases to signal culture rather than understanding (the 'quoting French on all occasions' example). A reader who only masters quotations or linguistic forms but not the ideas should not be credited with genuine appreciation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware confusing the pleasure of overcoming difficulty with aesthetic value
rubrics_metrics.description: Readers are 'apt to mistake' the pleasure attached to the sense of a difficulty overcome for a beauty inherent in the work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: readers who enjoy a foreign author because occasional passages become intelligible; they value the feeling of deciphering rather than the work's artistic merits. Evaluation should separate satisfactions from comprehension challenges vs. the work's intrinsic qualities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not revere canonical works solely for their status
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain books become 'standard' and 'the objects of this adoration'—works people feel a gentleman's library 'must' contain—leading many to bow before them without real acquaintance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-patterns: treating canonical texts as untouchable dogma; praising them because auctions or society declare them indispensable. Good practice: assess classics on their merits and on your own reading, not only their reputation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid praise motivated by social cowardice or fear of seeming foolish
rubrics_metrics.description: Much mock worship is due to 'abject cowardice' — a man who says he doesn't like a standard work 'runs... the risk of being thought a fool' and therefore keeps silent or feigns admiration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Indicator of sham admiration: public conformity of opinion, silence from dissenters, and castigating those who voice contrary views. Encourage honest expression; value independent judgments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Differentiate recollection/familiarity from active reading
rubrics_metrics.description: Many elderly people 'do not read [Shakespeare], but recollect him'—they are familiar with better-known beauties through performance or memory rather than engaged reading.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scoring should reward active engagement (close reading) over passive familiarity from performances or extracts; familiarity alone is an incomplete basis for deep critical judgment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize that required/classical education can produce artificial taste
rubrics_metrics.description: When young students are made to study poetry in Greek and Latin, their views 'are slightly artificial' — they may overvalue classical authors because much effort was expended on them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-pattern: preferring works because they were compulsory or prestigious in education rather than because of earned appreciation. Evaluate whether admiration arises from genuine response or from educational investment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value generosity, honesty, and pedagogy in criticism
rubrics_metrics.description: Leigh Hunt 'was never blind to the genius of an adversary... next to the pleasure he took in books was that he derived from teaching others to take pleasure in them.' Good critics impart knowledge and counter pretense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Positive criterion: critics who honestly appraise works regardless of authority, who teach others, and who help readers discern merits should be held up as models. Anti-pattern: critics who use authority to intimidate or to puff themselves up.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sham admiration harms authors, modern writers, and utterers themselves
rubrics_metrics.description: Sham admiration 'does their authors no good... is injurious not only to modern writers (who are generally made the subject of base comparison), but especially to the utterers of this false coin themselves.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluation should note the downstream effects: false praise diminishes honest discourse, handicaps contemporary writers, and degrades moral integrity of those who pretend.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be skeptical of boastful claims of having read everything
rubrics_metrics.description: Macaulay's 'every schoolboy knows' approach frightened many into pretending to know authors they had not read; boasting about exhaustive reading can intimidate others into false conformity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-pattern: intellectual posturing that pressures others to feign familiarity. Good critical practice favors humility and admitting limits of one's reading.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understand that some older works require contextual/scholarly knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: Many English authors of old date have beauties 'unintelligible except to those who are acquainted with the classics;' without that context, parts of such works may seem 'wearisome.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scoring nuance: lack of appreciation for such works may reflect missing background rather than poor taste; conversely, insistence on universal admiration despite intelligibility gaps is suspect. Encourage contextual education or honest acknowledgement of incomprehension.

rubrics_metrics.name: Encourage independent expression of opinion (courage to dissent)
rubrics_metrics.description: Instances like Miss Brontë's confessed dislike of Austen are praised as 'intrepidity'—women (and others) who courageously express genuine taste deserve respect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Positive criterion: value frank, independent judgments even when they contradict prevailing fashion. Anti-pattern: social shaming or 'bludgeoning' of dissenters by defenders of canonical taste.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware partial or selective admiration misread as comprehensive merit
rubrics_metrics.description: Readers often prize isolated passages or 'places' of intelligibility (e.g., Spenser excerpts) and mistake these for the overall merit of long, difficult works; 'the most tedious and even the most monstrous passages are often the most admired.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assessment should distinguish between admiration for excerpted highlights and evaluation of the whole work. Excerpt-based praise should be treated with caution.
